What is AWS Organizations and why use it?

AWS Organizations is a global service that groups multiple AWS accounts under a management account, organized into OUs. It provides consolidated billing (volume discounts, sharing of Reserved Instances and Savings Plans), automated account creation via API and, above all, central guardrails through SCPs. An example: separating Prod, Dev and Sandbox into different OUs with different rules. Precaution: the management account is not subject to SCPs, so you put as few workloads in it as possible.
How does an SCP work and what can it not do?

An SCP defines the permission ceiling for member accounts, inherited from the Root to the OUs and then the account. It never grants permissions: the action must be allowed by the SCP at every level AND by an IAM policy, and an explicit Deny always wins. For example, an SCP Deny dynamodb:* prevents all users in the OU, root user included, from using DynamoDB. It applies neither to the management account nor to service-linked roles.

What is the difference between a denylist and an allowlist strategy for SCPs?

In a denylist, you keep FullAWSAccess and add targeted Denies: it is simple and new services remain usable. In an allowlist, you detach FullAWSAccess and only allow listed services, with an Allow at every level of the hierarchy: it is stricter but heavier to maintain. I would choose the denylist by default and the allowlist for a highly regulated OU.
What is aws:PrincipalOrgID used for?

It is a condition key that you put in a resource-based policy (S3 bucket, SQS queue, KMS key...) to allow only principals from my organization, without listing the accounts. New accounts are covered automatically and an account that leaves the organization loses access. The policy must still contain an Allow with this condition.
Believing an SCP grants permissions: it only limits; without a matching IAM policy, nothing is allowed.
Forgetting that SCPs do NOT apply to the management account: you therefore cannot contain an administrator account there with an SCP.
In an allowlist, forgetting to have an Allow at every level (Root, OU, account): a single level without an Allow blocks everything.
Deleting FullAWSAccess without replacing it: no action is allowed anymore in the affected accounts.
Confusing a tag policy (standardizes keys/values, does not act on a missing tag) with the Config rule required-tags (detects the absence).
Thinking RI/Savings Plans discounts are shared unconditionally: sharing must be enabled on both accounts.
